passages.happening: Once again a huge crowd has gathered, and after three days with Jesus they have run out of food. Jesus says he feels for them. If he sends them home hungry, some will collapse on the road, because they have come from far away. The disciples ask where anyone could find bread out here. Jesus asks what they have. Seven loaves, and a few small fish. He has the people sit on the ground, gives thanks, breaks the bread, and hands it to the disciples to pass round. Everyone eats and is full, and seven large baskets of leftovers are gathered. About four thousand people were there. Then Jesus gets into the boat and crosses to a place called Dalmanutha.
passages.hearers:
This is the second feeding in Mark. The first, for five thousand, was in Jewish Galilee (6:30-44). This one seems to happen on the far side of the lake, near the Decapolis, the Greek cities where Jesus was in the last chapter (7:31). So the bread Jesus gave to Israel is now given to a crowd that likely included many Gentiles, people who were not Jews. The woman in Tyre asked for crumbs. Here there are baskets left over.

Mark even uses a different word for basket. After the first feeding the baskets were ordinary food baskets. Here the word is for a big hamper, the same word used in Acts for the basket in which Paul was lowered over the city wall of Damascus (Acts 9:25). It was large enough to hold a man.

No one today knows where Dalmanutha was. No other ancient writing names it. Matthew's account of the same trip says Magadan (Matthew 15:39), which is also unknown, and later copyists sometimes changed both names to Magdala, a known fishing town on the lake.
passages.ot: A crowd fed with bread in a lonely place would remind any Jew of the manna. God fed Israel in the desert, and “The Israelites ate manna forty years” (Exodus 16:35). The prophet Elisha once fed a hundred men with twenty loaves, and “They will eat and have some left over” (2 Kings 4:43). Jesus does what God did in the desert, and more than the prophets did.
passages.hard: Was this just the same story told twice? Some scholars think so, and point out how alike the two accounts are. Others note the differences: different numbers of people, loaves, and baskets, a different setting, and different words. Mark himself treats them as two events, because Jesus asks the disciples to remember both (8:19-20). Whatever view is taken, Mark wants his readers to set the two side by side.
passages.asks: The disciples had seen Jesus feed five thousand. Faced with a new crowd, they still asked, 'Where could anyone find bread?' It is easy to forget what God has already done. Ask what past help from God you have forgotten in your present need.

passages.t: A sign from heaven, and the one loaf
passages.happening: Some Pharisees come and argue with Jesus. To test him, they demand a sign from heaven. Jesus sighs deeply and says no sign will be given to this generation. He leaves them and crosses the lake again. In the boat the disciples realize they have brought only one loaf. Jesus warns them to watch out for the yeast of the Pharisees and of Herod. They think he is talking about their lack of bread. Jesus asks them question after question: Don't you see? Don't you understand? Are your hearts hard? When I fed the five thousand, how many baskets were left? Twelve. And the four thousand? Seven. “Do you still not understand?”
passages.hearers:
A 'sign from heaven' meant a public wonder that would prove a leader came from God. Jesus had already healed and fed thousands. But these men wanted proof on their own terms, a sign they could check and control. Jesus refuses to perform on demand.

Yeast, also called leaven, was a lump of old dough kept back to make the next batch rise. A tiny bit works through the whole loaf. So it became a picture of influence, often bad influence. At Passover every Jewish home removed all leaven (Exodus 12:15). Paul writes, “a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough” (1 Corinthians 5:6). Luke says the leaven of the Pharisees was hypocrisy (Luke 12:1).

The Herod here is Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee who had John the Baptist killed (6:14-29). The Pharisees wanted signs. Herod wanted power and silenced the prophet who troubled him. Mark leaves the reader to see what they share: hearts closed to what God is doing.
passages.ot: Jesus' question in verse 18 borrows the words of the prophets. Jeremiah spoke to people “who have eyes but do not see, who have ears but do not hear” (Jeremiah 5:21). Ezekiel said the same of a rebellious house (Ezekiel 12:2). Those words were spoken against Israel's unbelief. Now Jesus says them to his own disciples.
passages.hard: Why does Jesus press the numbers, twelve baskets and seven? Readers have long suggested meanings. Twelve may stand for the twelve tribes of Israel, and seven for fullness, or for the nations. Mark does not explain, and it is wise not to lean too hard on any one meaning. The plain point is clear: Jesus has given bread, more than enough, twice. And the disciples have one loaf with them in the boat. Many readers think Mark wants us to see that the one loaf they overlook is Jesus himself.
passages.asks: The disciples were anxious about bread while the one who fed thousands sat beside them. Ask what you are worrying about this week as if Jesus were not in the boat. And ask whether you, like the Pharisees, are asking God for proof he has already given.

passages.t: A blind man healed in two stages
passages.happening: At Bethsaida people bring a blind man to Jesus and beg him to touch him. Jesus takes the man by the hand and leads him out of the village. He spits on his eyes, puts his hands on him, and asks, “Can you see anything?” The man says, “I can see the people, but they look like trees walking around.” Jesus puts his hands on his eyes again, and now the man sees everything clearly. Jesus sends him home and tells him not to go back into the village.
passages.hearers:
Bethsaida was a fishing town at the north end of the lake. The Jewish historian Josephus says that Herod's son Philip raised it from a village to a city and renamed it Julias, after the emperor's daughter. Two sites near the shore each have their defenders as the real Bethsaida, and the question is still open.

This is the only healing in the Gospels that happens in two steps. Jesus is not failing the first time. Mark places this story right after Jesus asks his disciples, 'Having eyes, do you not see?' and right before Peter says who Jesus is. The man is a picture of the disciples. They see something, but blurred. They will need a second touch.

As with the deaf man in the last chapter, Jesus takes the man away from the crowd and heals him by touch. He leads him by the hand, the way you would lead a blind friend.
passages.ot: Isaiah promised that when God comes to save, “Then the eyes of the blind will be opened” (Isaiah 35:5). Mark has told of the deaf hearing in chapter 7. Now the blind see. Both halves of Isaiah's promise are coming true.
passages.hard: Why would Jesus need two tries? Mark does not say he did. The text reads more like a lesson than a struggle. Jesus asks a question in the middle, as a teacher would, and the man's honest answer, 'they look like trees', is part of the story. Many readers see the two stages as Mark's way of showing that sight comes in steps, for the disciples and for us.
passages.asks: The man was honest about seeing only in part. He did not pretend. Ask where your own sight of Jesus is still blurred, and whether you are willing to say so and ask for the second touch.

passages.happening: Jesus and his disciples walk north to the villages around Caesarea Philippi. On the way he asks them, “Who do people say I am?” They give the answers going round: John the Baptist, Elijah, one of the prophets. Then he asks, “But what about you?” and, “Who do you say I am?” Peter answers, “You are the Christ.” Jesus tells them not to tell anyone about him.
passages.hearers:
Caesarea Philippi lay well north of the Sea of Galilee, at the foot of Mount Hermon, beside a spring that feeds the Jordan. A cave there held a shrine to the Greek god Pan, and Herod the Great built a temple there in honour of the emperor Augustus. Herod's son Philip later rebuilt the town and named it Caesarea, after Caesar, adding his own name to set it apart from the Caesarea on the coast. It was a place full of other gods and of Rome's power. Here, of all places, Jesus asks who he is.

'Christ' is the Greek form of the Hebrew word Messiah. Both mean 'anointed one', a person marked out by God with oil for a task, as kings were. By Jesus' day many Jews hoped for an anointed king from the family of David. One Jewish writing from the century before Jesus, the Psalms of Solomon, prays for a son of David who would drive the foreign nations out of Jerusalem and rule God's people. That was the hope in many minds: a king who wins.

This is the turning point of Mark's book. The first line called Jesus the Christ (1:1). Now, halfway through, a disciple finally says it.
passages.ot: God promised David a son whose kingdom would last for ever (2 Samuel 7:12-16), and the prophets looked for a king from David's line. Peter's answer means: you are that king.
passages.hard: Why does Jesus tell them to keep quiet? The title was true, but the people had the wrong picture of it. If word spread that Jesus was the Messiah, crowds would expect a war against Rome. Jesus will first show them what kind of Messiah he is, as the next verses make plain.
passages.asks: Jesus moves from 'What do people say?' to 'What about you?' Opinions about Jesus are easy to report. He wants your own answer. Ask who you say he is, and whether your life agrees with your answer.

passages.t: The Son of Man must suffer
passages.happening: Now Jesus begins to teach them something new. The Son of Man must suffer many things, be rejected by the leaders in Jerusalem, be killed, and after three days rise again. He says it openly. Peter takes him aside and starts to scold him. Jesus turns, looks at the other disciples, and rebukes Peter in front of them: “Get behind Me, Satan!” and, “For you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men.”
passages.hearers:
The elders, chief priests, and scribes were the three groups that made up the Jewish ruling council in Jerusalem. Jesus is saying that Israel's own leaders will reject him.

This would have shocked the disciples. A Messiah was supposed to win. Years later Paul could still say that a crucified Messiah was “a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles” (1 Corinthians 1:23). Peter is not being wicked. He loves Jesus and thinks he is protecting him.

A disciple walked behind his teacher. He did not correct him in public. Peter takes Jesus aside, which reverses the order. Jesus' words 'Get behind me' use the same Greek as his first call, 'Come, follow me', which is literally 'come behind me' (1:17). Jesus is sending Peter back to his place as a follower.

The name Satan means 'adversary'. In the desert Satan tested Jesus (1:13). Peter, without meaning to, is offering the same thing: a crown without a cross.
passages.ot: The word 'must' points to God's plan in Scripture. Isaiah spoke of a servant who “was despised and rejected by men” and who “was pierced for our transgressions” (Isaiah 53:3, 5). A psalm says, “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Psalm 118:22), a verse Jesus will quote later in Mark (12:10). And Daniel saw “One like the Son of Man” given an everlasting kingdom (Daniel 7:13-14). Jesus joins the glory of Daniel's Son of Man to the suffering of Isaiah's servant.
passages.hard: Did Jesus really foresee his death and rising, or did the church add these words later? Some scholars since about 1900 have argued that the sayings were shaped after Easter. Others argue that Jesus, who knew the fate of the prophets and of John the Baptist, could well foresee his death and gave it meaning beforehand. Christians have always held that Jesus knew where he was going and went there on purpose. Mark tells it that way: he spoke 'quite frankly'.
passages.asks: Peter wanted a Jesus who would not suffer, and a road for himself without pain. Most of us want the same. Ask where you have tried to keep Jesus' blessings while refusing his way.

passages.happening: Jesus calls the crowd together with his disciples. Anyone who wants to come after him must deny himself, take up his cross, and follow him. Whoever tries to save his life will lose it. Whoever loses his life for Jesus and for the good news will save it. What good is it to gain the whole world and lose your soul? Nothing can buy it back. And whoever is ashamed of Jesus and his words now, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his Father's glory with the holy angels.
passages.hearers:
To us 'my cross to bear' can mean any small trouble. To Jesus' hearers the cross meant only one thing: the Roman death for slaves and rebels. After King Herod died in 4 BC, the Roman governor Varus put down a revolt and, Josephus says, crucified about two thousand men. Galileans knew what crucifixion looked like. A condemned man carried his own cross to the place of death. The Greek writer Plutarch mentions it in passing: every criminal who is punished carries his own cross. In 1968, in a tomb in Jerusalem, a bone box was found holding the heel bone of a crucified man named Yehohanan, with an iron nail still driven through it. 'Take up your cross' meant: walk the road of a condemned man.

The cross was also meant to shame. It stripped a man of honour in public. To be 'ashamed' of Jesus would mean siding with public opinion against a condemned man.

The word Jesus uses for 'life' and for 'soul' is the same Greek word, psychē. He is playing on it. Clutch your life, and you lose your soul. Give your life away, and you keep it.
passages.ot: A psalm says that no one can pay a ransom to God for a life: “For the redemption of his soul is costly, and never can payment suffice” (Psalm 49:8). Jesus asks the same question in the language of trade: “Or what can a man give in exchange for his soul?” The 'adulterous' generation echoes the prophets, who called Israel's turning to other gods unfaithfulness in marriage (Hosea 2; Jeremiah 3).
passages.hard: Does 'deny himself' mean hating yourself, or never enjoying anything? No. It means saying no to self as master. The self is not destroyed. It is handed over. Paul put it this way: “I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Jesus also promises that the one who loses his life for him will save it. The goal is not less life but true life.
passages.asks: Jesus says this to the crowd, not to a few heroes. Following him is for everyone, and it costs everyone something. Ask what 'saving your life' looks like for you: comfort, reputation, control. And ask what it would mean this week to let go of it for his sake.
